results.title: DigitalOcean raises H100, H200 and MI300X GPU Droplet prices about 30%
highlights:
From August 1, 2026, an H100 GPU Droplet costs $4.41 per GPU-hour on demand instead of $3.39. The L40S and RTX Ada Droplets kept their prices.

...

DigitalOcean raised the on-demand prices of its NVIDIA and AMD GPU Droplets on August 1, 2026. It announced the change in a blog post on July 21, 2026, and gave strong demand for advanced GPU capacity as the reason. The H100, H200 and AMD MI300X Droplets each went up about 30%.

## Old and new prices

On-demand price per GPU per hour. Each of these Droplets comes with 1 or 8 GPUs (the L40S and RTX Ada Droplets with 1).

| GPU | Until July 31 | From August 1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA HGX H200 | $3.44 | $4.47 |
| NVIDIA HGX H100 | $3.39 | $4.41 |
| AMD Instinct MI300X | $1.99 | $2.59 |
| NVIDIA L40S | $1.57 | $1.57 |
| NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada | $1.57 | $1.57 |
| NVIDIA RTX 4000 Ada | $0.76 | $0.76 |

The old prices are from DigitalOcean’s pricing page as it stood on July 22, 2026, when it said “New on-demand pricing is coming on August 1, 2026.” The page now also lists the AMD Instinct MI325X on demand at $3.80 per GPU-hour.

## Reserved prices

The blog post says 12-month reserved rates changed on August 1 too. If you signed a contract that locks your rate, it stays until the term ends; a renewal moves to the new reserved rate. The page now lists these 12-month reserved prices per GPU-hour: B300 $7.94, H200 $3.40, H100 $3.26, MI350X $4.76, MI325X $2.88 and MI300X $1.91.

## Who pays more

Every GPU Droplet running on or after August 1 is billed at the new rate. The higher charges first appeared on the bill dated September 1, 2026. DigitalOcean told customers who didn’t want the new rate to destroy their GPU Droplets by August 1. Powering a GPU Droplet off doesn’t stop the charges: the FAQ says you pay until you destroy it.

...

If you run an H100 Droplet around the clock, it now costs about $3,220 a month at $4.41 an hour, against about $2,380 at a 12-month reserved rate of $3.26. Compare both with what other GPU clouds charge before you commit for a year.

results.title: AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks Price Hike: Up 20% in 2026
highlights:
AWS raised the hourly rates of EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML by roughly 20% in July 2026, across six instance families (P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en and P4de), and the fourth rise of the year followed: on October 7, 2026 AWS raised the rates again, by 15% on most families, so that on eCorpIT’s page, read on November 2, 2026, P6-B300 bills at $16.146 per accelerator-hour outside GovCloud, up from $14.04 in July. The scope is Capacity Blocks, which AWS’s EC2 pricing page describes as a way to reserve GPU instances in advance for ML workloads. The July start date is reported two ways: AWS notified customers on June 26 of a July 1 start (TECHi), while eCorpIT says AWS’s own revised notice moved it to July 7. eCorpIT reports that AWS says the next update is due in January 2027.

...

| Date | What changed | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| January 3 | H200-linked rates up 15%: p5e.48xlarge from $34.61 to $39.80 an hour in most regions, and from $43.26 to $49.75 in US West (N. California) | eCorpIT |
| April 1 | 10% rise on US P5, P5en and P6-B200 rates | eCorpIT |
| July | About 20% on six families; effective July 1 per the June 26 notice, July 7 per AWS’s revised notice | TECHi, eCorpIT |
| October 7 | 15% on most families, about 26.5% on P5 and P5en outside the US | eCorpIT |
| January 2027 | Next update due, as AWS states it | eCorpIT |

...

The table lists the October 7 rate per accelerator-hour for each family, as eCorpIT reports the schedule. eCorpIT’s page, read on November 2, 2026, says AWS now lists one Capacity Block rate across regions, apart from GovCloud on P6, and puts P5 at $5.970 per accelerator-hour in all listed regions. AWS’s own Capacity Blocks pricing page also lists P4d, which is not among the six July families, at $1.696 per accelerator-hour for standard AWS regions, the cheapest Nvidia family on that schedule.

| Family | October 7 rate per accelerator-hour | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| P6-B300 | $16.146 | Outside GovCloud; up 15% from $14.04 in July |
| P6-B200 | $14.208 | Outside GovCloud; up 15% from $12.355 in July |
| P5 | $5.970 | All listed regions, per eCorpIT; up 15% from $5.191 in US regions and about 26.5% from $4.72 outside the US, July rates |
| P5e | $6.866 | Up 15% from $5.97 in July; used in the p5e.48xlarge series below |
| P5en | $7.895 | Outside GovCloud; up 15% from $6.865 in US regions and about 26.5% from $6.241 elsewhere, July rates |
| P4de | $2.546 | Outside GovCloud; up 15% from $2.214 in US regions in July |
| P4d | $1.696 | Standard AWS regions, from AWS’s Capacity Blocks pricing page |

...

Eight accelerators make an instance, so p5.48xlarge now costs $47.76 an hour ($5.970 times eight), and eCorpIT’s own figure for an eight-GPU B300 block at $16.146 is about $129 an hour. Tracing one instance through the steps shows the cumulative effect. The p5e.48xlarge cost $34.61 an hour before January 3 and $39.80 after it, per eCorpIT. Taking eight accelerators per instance, October’s $6.866 makes it $54.93 an hour, which is 58.7% above where the year began and well past the 38% TECHi counted after July.

...

A Capacity Block runs for 1 to 14 days or a multiple of 7 days up to 182 days, with up to 64 instances per block (512 GPUs at eight per instance), and it can be scheduled up to 8 weeks ahead, according to AWS’s Capacity Blocks documentation. AWS’s billing documentation says the block price is charged up front, with the payment landing on your account between 5 minutes and 12 hours after purchase. From the start of the block, the running charge is the operating system fee alone.

The OS charge is a separate line item. In AWS’s worked example, a reservation price of $31.464 per instance-hour produced a $6,041.088 reservation charge, and an operating-system price of $1.8432 per instance-hour produced a further $346.52. A budget built from the reservation rate alone comes up short, and the cash for the first line leaves the account within hours of booking.

...

AWS’s stated reason, as eCorpIT quotes it, is that Capacity Block pricing varies with supply and demand and that the adjustment “reflects the supply/demand patterns we expect this quarter.” Two outside voices split on that. Cloud economist Corey Quinn calls the change “a policy decision, not supply/demand”, on the grounds that AWS updated published base rates. Analyst Pareekh Jain says the “most defensible explanation is simply market-based pricing tied to supply and demand.”

...

Rank.ai’s November 10, 2026 snapshot lists on-demand p5.48xlarge at $55.04 an hour in us-east-1, or $6.88 per GPU-hour. A Capacity Block at the October 7 P5 rate of $5.970 per accelerator-hour is $47.76 an hour, 13% below that list price. On-demand P5 pricing was also cut earlier: as of November 13, 2026, AWS’s June 5, 2025 announcement says the P5 reduction of up to 45% applied to On-Demand pricing from June 1, 2025 and to Savings Plan purchases after June 4, 2025.

| GPU | Provider and product | Per GPU-hour | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | AWS Capacity Block (P5) | $5.970 | Rate from October 7 |
| H100 | AWS on-demand (p5.48xlarge, us-east-1) | $6.88 | Rank.ai, November 10 |
| H100 | Nebius on-demand | $4.50 | Raised October 1 |
| H200 | AWS Capacity Block (P5e) | $6.866 | Rate from October 7 |
| H200 | Nebius on-demand | $5.40 | Raised October 1 |
| B200 | AWS Capacity Block (P6-B200) | $14.208 | Rate from October 7 |
| B200 | Nebius on-demand | $8.50 | Raised October 1 |
| B300 | AWS Capacity Block (P6-B300) | $16.146 | Rate from October 7 |
| B300 | Nebius on-demand | $9.50 | Raised October 1 |

The Nebius figures come from Sesame Disk, which reports that Nebius raised on-demand GPU rates 17-21% on October 1, 2026; Nebius’s pricing page lists H100 at $4.50 and B300 at $9.50 per GPU hour. The same Sesame Disk report says CoreWeave added a 10% increase after a 25% rise in July, putting its pricing up roughly 37.5% since July. The neoclouds have been raising rates too. For Azure and Google Cloud H100 pricing, see our AWS, Azure and Google Cloud GPU pricing comparison, and for the H200 class on AMD’s side our AMD MI350P and Nvidia H200 comparison.

...

Convergedigest reports that customers pay the prevailing rate when the reservation is purchased, even if the reserved capacity starts after a future price change. AWS’s billing documentation agrees on the mechanics: a search across a range of dates returns the lowest-priced offering available, and once you have reserved a block its price does not change. With blocks bookable up to 8 weeks ahead, a block bought before the January 2027 update can start weeks later at the old rate. AWS gives only “January 2027” for that update, and the first 2026 rise landed on January 3, so do not assume you have the whole month. VentureBeat’s advice is to check Capacity Block rates before buying, since AWS has raised them four times in 2026.

Locking a rate is worth it only if you fill the block, because the whole block is charged up front. A block costs the same whether the GPUs are busy or idle, while on-demand bills only the hours used. The break-even utilisation is the block’s hourly price divided by the on-demand hourly price. For H100, $47.76 divided by $55.04 is 87%, so a block beats on-demand list only if you use at least 87% of its hours. A block also reserves the capacity, so 87% is the cost line and not the whole decision. The comparison sets the block’s reservation price against the on-demand rate and leaves out the separate OS fee.

results.title: Newer silicon is not always the smarter buy. | Spheron Network
highlights:
Newer silicon is not always the smarter buy.

$4.96/hr and $5.85/hr. Two GPUs, one generation apart, less than a dollar between them per hour. The cheaper option is last year's chip, and it might still be the right call for your workload.

Current Spheron marketplace pricing, subject to availability and may vary by region:

$4.96/hr is on-demand H200, with spot as low as $3.31/hr (33% off).

$5.85/hr is on-demand B300, the lowest bookable on-demand rate on the whole marketplace.

Here's how to choose:

Pick H200 if you run a proven Hopper-class training or inference pipeline and want the lowest cost per token today. The spot rate alone cuts a third off your bill.

Pick B300 instead if you need current-gen Blackwell Ultra silicon for newer model architectures and want the cheapest on-demand entry point on the platform.

results.title: What Happens When AI Providers Raise Prices to Reflect Their True Compute Costs? – aitechmodel.com
highlights:
When AI providers raise prices to reflect compute costs, they don't simply pass costs through—instead, they optimize margins differently for enterprise and consumer segments. The underlying driver is real: GPU memory now

...

AWS raised its H200 GPU instance prices by 15% in January 2026, marking the first major cloud GPU price hike in approximately two decades—a signal that these cost pressures are real and sustained. Similar increases have rolled out globally: Alibaba Cloud, Baidu AI Cloud, Tencent Cloud, and Google Cloud all raised AI compute and storage prices in the first half of 2026. The shortage is structural, not cyclical—tight supply is expected to persist unless AI demand cools significantly or new chip manufacturing capacity comes online.

...

The actual price moves tell a surprising story. Anthropic raised enterprise pricing by introducing a $20-per-seat base fee plus pay-per-token rates in April 2026, explicitly citing compute crunch as justification. Yet Anthropic simultaneously cut consumer token prices 67%, dropping Opus input tokens from $15 to $5 per million tokens in February 2026, while Google cut AI Ultra prices 20% for consumer users despite raising underlying infrastructure costs.

...

If you're running AI workloads at scale, GPU pricing is the real constraint. NVIDIA H100 pricing ranges from $1.49 per hour on specialized providers to $6.98 per hour on Azure's on-demand offering, depending on region, commitment terms, and provider.

A single inference-heavy workload demanding 100 GPUs running 24/7 for a month will cost roughly $36,000 to $168,000 in raw GPU compute alone—before networking, storage, or software licenses. API pricing appears cheaper per token, but only because providers absorb hyperscaler efficiencies and depreciate hardware across millions of requests. The underlying GPU cost per inference is still $1.49 to $6.98 per hour divided by inference throughput, meaning raw cost recovery favors high-volume enterprise usage over spot inference.

results.title: Daily Investment Brief — August 1, 2026 | Signwl
highlights:
The compute market is bifurcating along two axes simultaneously: architecture and geography. On architecture, NVIDIA-architecture public cloud capacity — L4 inference, L40S, H100 — is tightening in single-provider markets globally, with L4 SPOT repricing +20–277% across 14 regions in 30 days and the L40S in Mumbai up +110% over the same window. Yet AWS's own custom ASIC story is more complicated: Trainium SPOT is surging +305–435% in Melbourne and São Paulo, but those are non-US thin markets where residual pool mechanics dominate; the OD tier — the actual floor — sits flat at ~$0.94/hr across all core US regions. The "ASIC pricing floor" narrative that dominated the initial scan does not survive rigorous validation.

...

...

The regional pattern is the diagnostic tell. L4 SPOT is repricing in Sydney (+20.2% to $0.517/hr), Stockholm (+35.6% to $0.313/hr), Frankfurt (+26.9% to $0.356/hr), Seoul (+28.4% to $0.274/hr), and Jeddah (+47.2% to $0.344/hr) — all markets at meaningful absolute prices, all with n_providers = 1, all showing zero competitive downward pressure. The intraday +94.6% move in Oregon on July 30 is consistent with an institutional buyer sweeping available spot inventory in a single session. The L40S data confirms the trend is inference-GPU-wide: Mumbai up +110% to $1.33/hr over 30 days, Seoul L40S up +33.3% week-over-week. Critically, the two L4 markets that are declining — London (-39.0%) and Mumbai (-9.7%) — both have n_providers = 2, and London's spread has ballooned to 15,817%, the signature of a new entrant pricing aggressively. The competitive mechanism works instantly when a second provider enters; the problem is that most markets don't have one.

results.title: China GPU Prices Spike 30% as AI Demand Outstrips Supply: Procurement Strategy for Foreign Tech Firms | China Gateway 360
highlights:
Graphics processing unit (GPU) prices in China have spiked by an estimated 30-40% since June 2026 as breakneck demand for AI model training collides with tightening export controls and domestic supply bottlenecks. Procurement teams at foreign tech firms operating in China are reporting lead times of 8-12 weeks for NVIDIA H100-equivalent clusters, up from 3-4 weeks a year ago, while Chinese cloud providers have raised GPU-instance pricing by 25% in Q3 alone. If your China AI operations depend on compute, here’s what’s happening — and what to do about it.

...

## GPU Availability and Pricing Snapshot: July 2026

| GPU / Equivalent | Availability | Estimated Price (China, USD) | Lead Time |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA H20 (China-spec) | Limited allocation | $15,000-18,000/unit | 8-12 weeks |
| Huawei Ascend 910B | Available, priority to SOEs | $12,000-14,000/unit | 4-6 weeks |
| Cambricon Siyuan 590 | Available, growing | $8,000-10,000/unit | 2-4 weeks |
| Cloud GPU (A100-equiv, per hour) | Available, price rising | $3.80-4.50/hour | On-demand |
| Cloud GPU (H100-equiv, per hour) | Waitlist on major clouds | $6.50-8.00/hour | 2-4 weeks waitlist |

Cloud pricing has risen fastest. Alibaba Cloud’s GPU-accelerated ECS instances were repriced upward by 25% effective July 1, 2026, and Tencent Cloud followed with a 20% hike a week later. Reserved-instance discounts, which previously offered 40-50% off on-demand rates for 1-year commitments, have been reduced to 25-30%.

...

1. Cloud-first with multi-cloud hedging: If your AI workloads are bursty (training runs under 1,000 GPU-hours), cloud remains the pragmatic choice despite price hikes. Split workloads across Alibaba Cloud, Huawei Cloud, and AWS China (Beijing/Ningxia regions) to arbitrage availability. Set up automated spot-instance bidding — spot GPU instances are 60-70% cheaper than on-demand and increasingly available as providers add capacity.
2. Hybrid: Own inference, rent training: Inference workloads run efficiently on last-generation GPUs (NVIDIA A100, Huawei Ascend 910) or even on high-end consumer cards (RTX 4090, widely available in China at ¥14,000-16,000). Purchase inference hardware outright and allocate cloud budget exclusively to large training runs. This split typically reduces total compute spend by 35-45% compared to all-cloud.
3. Domestic GPU pilot program: If you have a 6-month runway, start a pilot on Huawei Ascend or Cambricon hardware. The software gap is narrowing fast — PyTorch 2.4 added native Ascend backend support in June 2026, and Cambricon’s Neuware SDK now supports ONNX model import. A small pilot (2-4 GPUs, 4-8 weeks) tells you whether domestic hardware can meet your inference or fine-tuning needs at 40-50% lower hardware cost.

results.title: Dedicated GPU server vs GPU cloud: hidden costs — DediGPU
highlights:
In short

- A month is 730 hours: the median on-demand H100 costs about $2,460 a month running; our H100 SXM is $1,134 whether it runs or not.
- The hourly price hides storage that keeps billing, egress, idle hours, pre-emption and shared hosts.
- Cloud for bursts and uncertainty; dedicated for anything that runs more than half the hours in a month.

...

## 730 hours

A month is 730 hours. The median on-demand H100 in 2 September 2026 was $3.37 an hour, which is $2,460 a month if the instance runs continuously; the cheapest in-stock offer was $1.73, or $1,263. Our H100 SXM is $1,134 a month, whether it runs or not. The cloud is cheaper for any workload that runs less than 336 hours a month at the median rate, or 655 at the cheapest. Most serving workloads and most multi-week training runs are above both.

Storage

Cloud volumes bill whether the instance runs or not, at $0.08 to $0.20 per GB per month. A 2 TB dataset is $160 to $400 a month before compute. On a dedicated server, 1.5 TB of NVMe per H100 is in the price.

Egress

$0.05 to $0.09 per GB at the large clouds. Moving a 500 GB checkpoint out five times a month is $125 to $225. Ours is $0.

Idle time

An instance you forget to stop bills at full rate. A server billed by the month cannot surprise you.

Pre-emption

Spot capacity is cheap because it can vanish mid-run. A dedicated server is yours for the term; the only interruption we allow ourselves is announced maintenance under four hours a month.

...

Many cloud GPU instances are virtual machines on hosts shared with other tenants: PCIe bandwidth, CPU and network are contended. A dedicated server has one tenant.

...

| | DediGPU | Dedicated GPU hosts | GPU clouds |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1× H100, per month | $1,134 — the cost sheet | $1,230 – $2,099 | $2,460 (median on-demand ×730 h) |
| 1× RTX 4090, per month | $138 | $274 – $323 | $307 (median on-demand ×730 h) |
| How the price is set | published cost, zero margin | cost plus margin, unpublished | market rate, changes weekly |
| Setup fee | $0 | $0 – $99 | $0 |
| Minimum term | one month, no notice | one to twelve months | none |
| GPU dedicated to you | yes, whole server | yes | often shared hosts |
| Egress | $0 | metered above a quota | $0.05 – $0.09 per GB |
| Identity check | none | ID + card, usually | full KYC, credit card |
| Payment | crypto balance | card, wire, PayPal | card |

Dedicated-host figures are the published monthly prices of Latitude.sh, GPU-Mart and HostKey for a single-card server on 2 September 2026; cloud figures are the median on-demand rate tracked by getdeploying.com the same day, times 730 hours.

...

- Bursts. A hyper-parameter sweep that needs 64 GPUs for six hours is a cloud job. Nobody rents 64 cards for a month for that.
- Uncertainty. If you do not know whether you need a GPU at all next week, pay by the hour until you do.
- Managed services. Notebooks, pipelines, model registries and the people who run them. We rent hardware.
- Compliance paperwork. If your customer needs a SOC 2 report from the GPU provider, a crypto-only host with no KYC is not it.

results.title: MI350P vs H200 NVL: Behind on BF16, Ahead on GPT-OSS
highlights:
## AMD’s footnote prices an MI350P server at $327,238.40; a year of H200 rental costs $57,553 on demand at Verda

As checked on 12 November 2026, a footnote to AMD’s 23 July 2026 press release gives two dollar figures. One is an internal AMD estimate of $327,238.40 for an MI350P-based server. The other is $265,928.24 for an RTX PRO 6000-based server, which AMD describes as a public list price reported on an OEM website as of 16 July 2026. Both are whole-server prices, but one is an estimate and the other a list price, so read the gap between them with that difference in mind.

For the rival card there is a rental rate from one provider. Verda lists H200 instances with NVLink at $6.57 an hour on demand and $3.29 an hour spot, per GPU. A continuous year is 8,760 hours (365 times 24), and the table converts the two rates into an annual cost.

| Verda H200 rate | Price per GPU hour | One continuous year (8,760 hours) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On demand | $6.57 | $57,553 |
| Spot | $3.29 | $28,820 |

Read the rows as a yardstick for any quote, not a forecast, and swap in your own provider’s rate where it differs from Verda’s. A card priced against a year of on-demand H200 time at $57,553 has to run a large share of the year to beat renting. The comparison is also incomplete in both directions: the card still needs a server, power and support, while Verda’s rate covers a complete GPU instance. Prices also move, as our report on Nvidia’s GPU price hike covers, so date every quote you collect.
